title: Goodbye — and how to survive when you run out of words
goal: Wind up a conversation, offer congratulations, and keep going when words fail you — while learning the last case, the vocative, used for addressing people.
bekal: addressing people with the right vocative form
offering congratulations and good wishes for almost any occasion
keeping a conversation going by asking for repetition, filling pauses and admitting you don't understand

notes: ***Profesorice* and *sine* are vocative forms** — the seventh and last case, used only for addressing people. You've met it since Unit 1 (*Emire!*) without explanation; now the full rule is below, and it's the easiest of the seven.

***Hvala vam na svemu* — *hvala na* + locative.** To thank someone for something specific: *hvala na pomoći* (thanks for your help), *hvala na pozivu* (for the invitation), *hvala na svemu* (for everything). Notice too that *hvala vam* uses the dative — two cases in one short sentence.

***Ako budem imao vremena* is the future II**, a tense used after *ako* and *kada* for actions that aren't certain yet. The formula is *budem / budeš / bude…* + the *-o / -la* form. You don't need to produce it yet; just recognize that it exists and that it means "if it turns out that…".

***Jezik se zaboravlja brzo* — a subjectless sentence with *se*,** exactly the pattern from Unit 12: *ovdje se ne puši*, *kako se kaže*. Bosnian uses *se* to say something that's true in general, without pointing at anyone.

***Čuvaj se!*** literally means "guard yourself" and is a warm farewell, used with people you care about or respect. Together with *Sretno!* (good luck) and *Sve najbolje!* (all the best), it closes a conversation far better than *doviđenja* on its own.

grammars.title: Vokativ — addressing people
body: The last case, and the only one that's never part of the sentence: it stands alone, set off by a comma, and has only one job — calling someone.

head: Type
Nominative
Vocative
Example
rows: **m ending in č, ć, š, ž, j, lj, nj, c**

after: **Women's names are often left as they are in everyday speech.** *Amina, hajde!* sounds natural; *Amino!* is grammatically correct but sounds more formal or regional. Men's names, on the other hand, almost always change: *Emire, Edine, Harise*. Foreign names like *Budi* are usually left alone, and nobody will correct you.

**Polite forms of address you'll use and hear every day:** *Gospodine!* (sir), *Gospođo!* (ma'am), *Gospođice!* (miss — less and less used), *Doktore!*, *Profesore!* / *Profesorice!*, *Kolega!* / *Koleginice!*

**Very Bosnian friendly forms of address:** *Brate!* (bro — used between men who aren't actually brothers), *Sine!* (son — from older to younger people), *Dušo!* (darling — used far more freely than in English, even by shopkeepers to customers), *Šefe!* (boss — half joking), *Komšija!* (neighbor).
**The vocative isn't used for things** except in poems and songs. And it never takes a preposition — if there's a preposition, it's a different case.

grammars.title: Surviving when you run out of words
body: This is the most practical part of the whole course. Real conversations don't fail because your grammar is wrong, but because you stop. The sentences below keep a conversation alive.

head: To…
Bosanski
Meaning
rows: Well… / So… / How should I put it…
I'm learning Bosnian, I've only just started.
Is that right? / Do you understand me?
I have to go. Talk soon!

after: **One sentence that changes the whole conversation: *Učim bosanski.*** Say it at the start, not after you've stumbled. Bosnians almost never meet foreigners learning their language, and the reaction is consistent: they slow down, they smile, and they help. This sentence is more useful than half the grammar in this course.
**Don't apologize over and over.** One *Izvinite* is enough; then carry on. Constant apologizing shifts attention from what you want to say to your language skills — and nobody is keeping score.

**Filler words are important, not a flaw.** *Pa…*, *znači…*, *ovaj…*, *kako da kažem…* buy you time to think while showing that your sentence isn't finished. Native speakers use them all day. Without them, your pauses sound like giving up.
**If all else fails, point and name it.** *Ovo, molim.* *Kako se ovo zove?* These two sentences work in shops, markets, restaurants and pharmacies — and you've known both since Unit 3.

sections.title: Čestitke i želje — congratulations and good wishes

blocks.text: In Bosnia, good wishes aren't small talk but part of the courtesy people expect. Skipping *prijatno* when someone starts eating, or *sretan put* when someone sets off, feels like something is missing.

head: Bosanski
Say it
When to say it
rows: Good luck! (before an exam, an interview)
Enjoy your meal! / Have a nice day

blocks.text: Two words that almost always go with good wishes: **hvala** to accept, and **također** (likewise, same to you) to return them. *Sretan put! — Hvala, također!* A more casual and very Bosnian form: *I tebi!* (you too).

blocks.title: Merhaba, selam, zdravo — three greetings, one city
items: In Sarajevo you'll hear all three side by side, and none of them is a wrong choice. ***Zdravo*** is neutral and safe everywhere. ***Merhaba*** is warm and typically Bosnian. ***Selam*** (or *Selam alejkum*) is used among Muslims and answered with *Alejkumu selam*.
If in doubt, *dobar dan* is never wrong. But saying *merhaba* with the right tone is one of the fastest ways to sound like someone who actually lives in this city, not just passing through.

blocks.text: Cover the Bosnian column, read the English, and rebuild the sentence from memory. This is the last wave review in the course — after this, your review is real conversation.
